title: "Writing a Voiceover Script: Pace, Pauses and Plain Words" (blog explainer)

brief.story: A clear explainer of the post.

slides.title: Voiceover Scripts: Pace, Pauses and Plain Words
slides.notes: A voiceover script is text that nobody reads. They only hear it, once, at the speed it's spoken. That changes the rules.

slides.title: Use sentence length as a dial
bullets: Longer sentences carry the listener along
slides.notes: Short sentences add weight. Longer ones carry the listener along. And give each sentence just one idea, so nobody has to hold two at once.

slides.title: Punctuation is your pause control
bullets: Question mark: tone change and pause
Pause before the number, not after
slides.notes: Full stops and questions create pauses. Use them to set up what you want remembered. So how many finished the study? Just over half.

slides.title: Swap jargon for plain words
slides.notes: Spoken jargon is harder to decode, because there's no time to stop. Say use, not utilise. Help, not facilitate. Define technical terms once.

slides.title: Tell listeners where they are
bullets: Transition: now, what did we try?
slides.notes: Preview what's coming, mark each transition, then recap. It feels repetitive on paper. In audio, it's what keeps people with you.

slides.title: From script to narrated slide video
bullets: Script lives in your speaker notes
Choose a voice and speaking speed
slides.notes: Put your script in the speaker notes. On Pro, a.i. directs the video and times the animation to your voice. Try it at powerpoint2vid.com.
